body:
FINDING (two CONFIRMED mechanisms, found by independent P5 lenses on T66's diff, 2026-07-25). The boot sweep's condemned set is computed from what a read can SEE, and §25 row quarantine means a read deliberately cannot see everything. Every erasure decision on the boot path therefore rests on a set that may be silently incomplete, in BOTH directions.

THE DERIVATION. `cmdServe` builds it from two reads — `backend.deltasSince(new Set())` on the primary and `archive.deltasSince(new Set())` — and hands the union to `tombstonesIn` (`src/cli/cli.ts:255-258`), which ingests exactly what it is given into a throwaway reactor and defers to `readTombstones` (`src/gateway/erase.ts:189-193`). But `SqliteBackend.deltasSince` SKIPS a row that fails admission (`src/store/sqlite.ts`, the §25 pen) and `LocalStorageBackend` does the same. A quarantined row contributes to no view — which is exactly right for a claim, and load-bearing wrong for a TOMBSTONE or for the NEGATION OF a tombstone.

DIRECTION 1 — A CORRUPT TOMBSTONE UN-ERASES ITS TARGET. Sequence, needing only a lagging archive at one moment: the operator erases `X`; the archive is unreachable just then, so the tombstone never reaches it and the archive's purge of `X` fails (the exact pair `heal(exclude)` exists to finish later); later the primary's tombstone row corrupts and joins the pen; on the next `serve --archive`, `dead` has no `X`, so `X` is not swept AND — worse — the archive's surviving copy is offered back through `replant`, planting the erased delta into the primary. `X` is then live at the REST and public doors with no strike anywhere.

DIRECTION 2 — A CORRUPT FORGIVENESS DESTROYS A FORGIVEN DELTA. `survivingTombstones` treats a lawful negation of a tombstone as FORGIVENESS (`erase.ts:148-159`: `if (!isTombstone(...) || negated(delta.id)) continue`), so a struck tombstone means its target is NOT dead. Now corrupt that forgiveness negation `N`: `N` is quarantined, so it never joins `alive`, so `toMirror` can NEVER archive it and the archive can never acquire a copy. Tombstone `T` therefore reads unstruck, its target `X` lands in `dead`, and heal purges `X` from BOTH tiers. A delta the operator deliberately un-erased is destroyed, irreversibly, and nothing says so.

WHAT T66 ALREADY DID ABOUT IT (do not rebuild these; build on them). PR for T66 closed the reachable half at the mirror: `heal` now WITHHOLDS its entire plant when the pen holds an `unparseable` row, on the stated ground that such a row may be a lawful tombstone nobody can read — withholding is recoverable, resurrection is not; it withholds by name any delta a still-penned row claims to strike; and `RestoreReport.stranded` now names EVERY row still set aside after a heal, including the ones no healthy copy exists for, which is the shape both lenses asked for. What T66 deliberately did NOT touch is the derivation itself, because that is a decision about what §11 promises when the ground is partly illegible, and it belongs to whoever owns that surface.

THE REAL QUESTION FOR THIS TICKET, and it is a design question before it is a code one: WHAT SHOULD THE CONDEMNED SET DO WHEN PART OF THE GROUND IS UNREADABLE? Three candidate answers, and the choice is what needs settling (Myk):
  (a) FAIL CLOSED ON THE SWEEP — a non-empty pen makes the boot sweep refuse to purge anything, on the ground that an unreadable row may be a forgiveness. Safe against direction 2, useless against direction 1, and it strands every legitimate erasure behind one corrupt row.
  (b) FAIL CLOSED ON BOTH, PER-ID — teach the derivation to report UNCERTAINTY rather than a set: `{ dead, uncertain }`, where `uncertain` is non-empty whenever a pen row could not be parsed. Callers then neither purge nor plant an uncertain id. This is the honest shape and the most work.
  (c) READ THE PEN'S BYTES FOR TOMBSTONE SHAPE — an `id-mismatch` / `invalid-signature` row HAS parsed claims (that is how T57 reads its `negates`), so the derivation could see that a penned row is tombstone-shaped or strikes a tombstone, and refuse to act on that lineage. Cheapest real coverage, and it does nothing for `unparseable`.

NOTE that (c) needs `QuarantinedRow` to carry more than it does — it has `key`, `reason`, `preview`, `negates` today, and deliberately not the claims (a pen row must not be laundered back into a delta). Widening it is a §25 decision, not an implementation detail: the whole point of the pen is that its contents are NOT trusted. `negates` is already the precedent for exposing a narrow, non-launderable fact about a penned row, so a `tombstones?: readonly string[]` companion is the shape most in keeping — but it is still a decision.

RAILS (both levels, and both directions — a rail for one direction is how this survived):
- Direction 1, end to end: erase `X` with a lagging archive so its purge fails there; corrupt the tombstone row; `serve --archive`; assert `X` is NOT readable through a Schema and NOT served at the REST/public doors, and that `holds(X)` is honest about the archive tier. This fails today.
- Direction 2, end to end and TWO-SIDED: erase `X`, forgive it with a lawful negation, corrupt the forgiveness row, `serve --archive`; assert `X` SURVIVES on both tiers (the bytes are still there) AND a named bystander erasure still completes in the same boot — a rail that only proved survival could pass by disabling the sweep.
- Unit, on whatever the derivation becomes: a pen holding an unreadable row yields uncertainty (or a refusal), never a confident set.

CARE: this is the irreversible direction on the most destructive subsystem in the stack, and it can WIDEN WHAT GETS PURGED or NARROW it depending on which answer is chosen — so per CLAUDE.md this is MYK'S MERGE either way, and the PR must state in one line what can now be deleted that could not before. Do not soften erasure's stated guarantee to make the fix easy: the promise is settled (2026-07-25) and this ticket is about keeping it when the ground is illegible, not about relaxing it.
title: The condemned set is derived from READABLE deltas only — a corrupt row silently un-erases (and a corrupt forgiveness silently destroys)
